title: 50,000 'Cockroach' Protesters March on Parliament as India's Monsoon Session Opens in Chaos
excerpt: Police fired tear gas and baton-charged demonstrators demanding the education minister's resignation over the NEET paper leak, as both houses of Parliament were adjourned amid the uproar.
body:
• Around 50,000 protesters from the Cockroach Janta Party marched toward Parliament on the opening day of India's monsoon session, demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation
  • Police fired tear gas and resorted to baton charges to prevent demonstrators from breaching barricades near the Parliament complex
  • Both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha were adjourned multiple times as opposition parties raised the NEET paper leak and alleged Ram Temple donation theft
  • Health Minister JP Nadda met CJP representatives and committed to discussing their demands within the government

The Biggest Challenge to Modi's Third Term

India's monsoon session of Parliament opened in chaos on Monday as approximately 50,000 protesters from the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party descended on central Delhi, attempting to march on the Parliament complex in what Reuters described as the biggest public challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi in his third term.

https://x.com/TheWeekLive/status/2079230834075459763

Delhi Police, which had denied permission for the march, deployed thousands of officers and paramilitary personnel across the capital. Demonstrators waving national flags and chanting "Dharmendra Pradhan quit" and "Narendra Modi quit" tried to breach metal barricades placed along routes from Jantar Mantar — their month-long protest site — to Parliament, just a few hundred metres away.

Police responded with tear gas and baton charges. Reuters journalists at the scene reported rounds of tear gas fired near Parliament to disperse crowds, while some protesters hurled stones at police.

""Thousands of students have gathered at Jantar Mantar for this cause."

"They've made it like North Korea."

— Abhijeet Dipke, Cockroach Janta Party founder, addressing protesters after police action

Parliament Washed Out on Day One

Inside Parliament, the opposition seized on the drama unfolding outside. Lok Sabha proceedings began at 11 am but lasted only seven to eight minutes before being adjourned to noon due to protests by opposition MPs. The house was adjourned five more times during the day. Rajya Sabha was adjourned for the entire day.

Congress leader Mallikarjun Kharge attempted to raise the NEET paper leak issue in the upper house before proceedings were suspended. "Thousands of students have gathered at Jantar Mantar for this cause. A lathi-charge has taken place there," Kharge told the house. "The government is trying to use force, suppress voices, and drive them away."

Opposition MPs also raised allegations of donation theft at the Ram Temple in Ayodhya, further fuelling disruptions. The government managed to introduce only one bill — a Supreme Court amendment to increase the number of judges from 34 to 38 — before proceedings collapsed. A bill to make insulting Vande Mataram a punishable offence could not be introduced in Rajya Sabha.

From Meme to Mass Movement

The Cockroach Janta Party began as a satirical online response after India's Chief Justice compared unemployed youth to "cockroaches" during an unrelated hearing in May. Supporters embraced the insult, turning it into a movement that the Wall Street Journal reported has attracted millions of followers on social media.

The movement was galvanised after the NEET-UG medical entrance exam papers were leaked in May, forcing some two million students to resit the examination. At least 12 students took their own lives in the aftermath, according to media reports, unable to face the ordeal of sitting the exam again.

The immediate trigger for Monday's escalation was the police decision on Saturday to forcibly move hunger-striking activist Sonam Wangchuk to hospital. The 59-year-old Ladakhi activist and engineer — the inspiration for the Bollywood film "3 Idiots" — joined the CJP sit-in last month and began a hunger strike that is now in its 23rd day. His hospitalisation brought thousands of supporters streaming to Jantar Mantar overnight.

Government Blinks — Slightly

In a potential shift, Health Minister JP Nadda met CJP representatives at his residence on Monday. Spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka said the party placed three demands: the immediate release of Sonam Wangchuk, Pradhan's resignation, and compensation of ₹1 crore for families of NEET aspirants who died by suicide.

However, Ranka later said the government had not responded to their specific demands. CJP spokesperson Saurav Das wrote on X: "Our demands are clear. The youth have gathered in huge numbers. We shall win!"

For NRI families with children in India's education system, the NEET crisis has been particularly alarming. The exam is the sole gateway to medical education in the country, and repeated leaks have shaken confidence in the system's integrity. Protest leader Dipke vowed demonstrations would continue until Pradhan resigns.
image_caption: Activist Sonam Wangchuk, whose hospitalisation during a hunger strike galvanised Monday's massive protest. The 59-year-old is on his 23rd day of fasting in solidarity with the student-led movement.
nri_angle: The NEET paper leak directly affects students seeking to study medicine in India, including NRI families with children pursuing medical education through the Indian exam system.
author: Diaspora Desk
